headline: New Orleans eats by the calendar (king cake, then crawfish, then sno-balls), and its proudest kitchens are Black Creole and Vietnamese, which makes food the most precise seasonal clock Nike has for Pelicans city product.
summary: New Orleans keeps time by what is in season: king cake from Twelfth Night to Mardi Gras, crawfish through Lent and Jazz Fest, sno-balls all summer, gumbo when the weather turns. The institutions that carry it are Black Creole (Dooky Chase's, Willie Mae's), neighborhood (Parkway, Leidenheimer, Hansen's) and Vietnamese (Dong Phuong in New Orleans East), and the street food of second-line Sundays (yakamein, huckabucks) runs on the same October-to-June clock as the NBA. The Pelicans already own one great food joke, the King Cake Baby, and play in an arena named for a smoothie chain born in metro New Orleans. Coming off 26-56, with first-year coach Jamahl Mosley and low expectations, city-pride product will carry this season more than roster product, and food is the sharpest way to time it. Every food collab needs paid local partners and food-brand licensing.

insights.title: Carnival is the Pelicans' food season
insights.detail: King cake season runs from Twelfth Night (Jan 6) to Mardi Gras Day (Feb 9, 2027), right through the heart of the home schedule, and locals argue over cakes from Dong Phuong, Haydel's and Manny Randazzo. The Pelicans already own the food's best inside joke: the unnerving King Cake Baby mascot that has haunted Carnival-season games since 2015.
insights.implication: Build the season's biggest city-specific drop around king cake rather than generic beads: release it on Jan 6, use the team-owned King Cake Baby, and pay a local bakery to make the co-branded box.

insights.title: Tremé's Black Creole kitchens are civic institutions
insights.detail: Leah Chase's Dooky Chase's fed Freedom Riders and civil rights organizers and still serves gumbo z'herbes on Holy Thursday (Mar 25, 2027). Willie Mae's Scotch House, a few blocks away, is the city's fried-chicken benchmark. Both sit in the Tremé and Seventh Ward corridor that the I-10 Claiborne overpass cut through in the 1960s.
insights.implication: The deepest food story in this market is Black Creole and family-owned, so tell it only through paid partnerships with these families and send proceeds back to the Claiborne corridor.

insights.title: The po-boy is a labor story on Central City bread
insights.detail: Locals trace the name to the 1929 streetcar strike, when ex-conductors Bennie and Clovis Martin fed striking 'poor boys' for free, and the loaf has come from Leidenheimer on Simon Bolivar Avenue in Central City since 1896. Ordering is coded: 'dressed' means lettuce, tomato, pickle and mayo, and 'debris' is the roast-beef gravy at Parkway.
insights.implication: A working-class origin story fits a team in a lean year. Use the butcher-paper wrap, the order ticket and the strike story for packaging and naming, and time it to the November Oak Street Po-Boy Festival.

insights.title: Vietnamese New Orleans makes Tết a home-market moment
insights.detail: Refugees who arrived after 1975 built Village de l'Est in New Orleans East around Mary Queen of Vietnam church, whose Tết festival falls near Lunar New Year (Feb 6, 2027), inside Carnival. Dong Phuong's loaves carry the city's banh mi ('Vietnamese po-boys') and its king cake sells out every year, while the West Bank (Gretna, Harvey) has its own pho-and-grocery corridor.
insights.implication: A Lunar New Year piece here is local, not borrowed from a coastal playbook: co-design it with Vietnamese New Orleanian artists and Dong Phuong instead of using generic zodiac graphics.

insights.title: Second-line Sundays come with their own menu
insights.detail: From late summer to spring, Social Aid and Pleasure Club parades through Tremé, the Seventh Ward and Central City are trailed by yakamein ('Old Sober') vendors, led in public by Ms. Linda Green, the Ya-Ka-Mein Lady, while front porches sell huckabucks (frozen Kool-Aid cups). The season lines up almost exactly with the NBA's.
insights.implication: This is Black neighborhood culture, not set dressing: engage through Feed the Second Line and paid collabs with vendors and clubs, and never print club names or regalia without permission.

insights.title: The arena and the beer are already food brands
insights.detail: Fans watch games in an arena named for Smoothie King, founded in metro New Orleans in 1973, and owner Gayle Benson owns Faubourg Brewing in New Orleans East, renamed from Dixie Beer in 2020 over the name's Confederate associations. Pelicans game day is a quick downtown pre-game crowd; the big tailgate culture belongs to the Saints next door.
insights.implication: Food collabs must clear the team's naming and beverage partners first, and activation should sit in the arena and along the Poydras corridor rather than in a parking-lot tailgate.

insights.title: Crawfish and sno-balls bookend the stretch run
insights.detail: Crawfish boils peak from March to May, through Lenten fish fries and Jazz Fest (Crawfish Monica, cochon de lait po-boys). Sno-ball stands like Hansen's Sno-Bliz (since 1939) reopen in spring with nectar cream, a pink vanilla-almond flavor found almost nowhere else.
insights.implication: Give the late season and any play-in run its own palette, boiled-crawfish red and nectar pink, instead of reusing Carnival purple, green and gold.

places.name: Dooky Chase's Restaurant
places.why: Leah Chase's Creole dining room, where civil rights strategy was planned over gumbo, is the most respected food address in Black New Orleans.

places.name: Willie Mae's Scotch House
places.why: Its fried chicken was named a James Beard America's Classic in 2005, and volunteers rebuilt it after Katrina, so it stands for neighborhood recovery.

places.name: Parkway Bakery & Tavern
places.why: Since 1911 it has been the roast beef debris and fried shrimp po-boy that locals take visitors to, and its T-shirts are worn around town.

places.name: Leidenheimer Baking Company
places.why: It has baked the thin-crust French bread under most of the city's po-boys since 1896.

places.name: Dong Phuong Bakery
places.why: Its banh mi loaves and butter-and-cream-cheese king cake draw lines from every corner of the metro.

places.name: Hansen's Sno-Bliz
places.why: This family stand, open since 1939, is the reference point for shaved-ice sno-balls and house-made syrups like nectar cream.

places.name: Café Reconcile
places.why: It trains young New Orleanians for hospitality jobs over red beans and fried catfish on the Oretha Castle Haley corridor, which makes it a natural community partner.

places.name: Hong Kong Food Market
places.why: It anchors Vietnamese and pan-Asian grocery shopping on the West Bank, the other half of the city's Vietnamese food map.

places.name: Turkey and the Wolf
places.why: Mason Hereford's sandwich shop has hand-scrawled, irreverent merch that young locals wear as a style signal.

places.name: Smoothie King Center
places.why: The home court is named for a smoothie chain founded in metro New Orleans, and its concession and beverage partners set the limits for any in-arena food collab.

people.name: Dooky Chase's (the Chase family)
people.role: Tremé restaurant family of Leah Chase (1923-2019), the 'Queen of Creole Cuisine'
people.why: Leah's grandson, chef Edgar 'Dook' Chase IV, and the family keep up the Holy Thursday gumbo z'herbes and a dining room hung with African American art, so any Creole-pride product should start with their consent.

people.name: Ms. Linda Green, the Ya-Ka-Mein Lady
people.why: Her yakamein at second lines and Jazz Fest, along with TV appearances with Anthony Bourdain and on Chopped, made 'Old Sober' a citywide symbol of Black New Orleans street food.

people.name: Nina Compton
people.role: Saint Lucian-born chef of Compère Lapin; 2018 James Beard Best Chef: South
people.why: She was a finalist on Top Chef's New Orleans season and became the city's leading Caribbean-Creole voice, linking New Orleans to the wider Black Atlantic table.

people.name: Serigne Mbaye
people.why: His tasting menu cooks the West African roots of Creole food (okra, rice, and gumbo's own name), a high-end voice for the diaspora story.

people.name: Mason Hereford
people.role: Chef-owner of Turkey and the Wolf and Molly's Rise and Shine
people.why: His thrift-store, hand-drawn design language and Bon Appétit's 2017 Best New Restaurant title turned a sandwich shop into a style reference for young locals.

people.name: Hubig's Pies
people.why: Its Savory Simon mascot became a cult T-shirt in the decade the pies were gone after the 2012 bakery fire, before they returned in 2022, proof that locals wear food brands as loyalty.

people.name: Krewe of Red Beans / Feed the Second Line
people.role: Lundi Gras bean-mosaic parade krewe and the culture-bearer nonprofit it started (founder Devin De Wulf)
people.why: The krewe turns a Monday dish into costume art and the nonprofit sends money to Black Masking Indians, second-line club members and musicians, which makes them a credible partner for red-beans product.

people.name: Poppy Tooker
people.role: Host of WWNO's 'Louisiana Eats!' and food historian
people.why: As the city's best-known food explainer, she is the right person to check a food story before it goes on product.

moments.name: King cake season (Twelfth Night to Mardi Gras)
moments.why: It runs through prime home dates, king cakes fill every office, and the King Cake Baby comes out at Pelicans games.

moments.name: Tết at Mary Queen of Vietnam
moments.why: New Orleans East's biggest community gathering, full of food stalls, lands inside Carnival.

moments.name: Red Beans Parade (Krewe of Red Beans)
moments.why: Bean-mosaic costumes parade through the downtown neighborhoods, turning Monday's dish into wearable art.

moments.name: Holy Thursday gumbo z'herbes at Dooky Chase's
moments.why: Leah Chase's Lenten green gumbo is the year's most coveted lunch, a late-season story moment.

moments.name: Crawfish season and Lenten Friday fish fries
moments.timing: Peaks March to May; Lenten Fridays Feb 12 - Mar 26, 2027
moments.why: Backyard boils and church fish fries are where fans gather during the stretch run.

moments.name: New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival
moments.timing: Last weekend of April and first weekend of May, Fair Grounds
moments.why: Its food booths (Crawfish Monica, cochon de lait po-boys, Ms. Linda's yakamein) are a city ritual that collides with play-in and playoff dates.

moments.name: Treme Creole Gumbo Festival
moments.why: This free festival pairs gumbo with brass bands in Tremé during the first month of the season.

moments.name: Oak Street Po-Boy Festival
moments.why: A street festival for the city's sandwich and a natural launch for po-boy product.

vocabulary.meaning: A po-boy with lettuce, tomato, pickles and mayo; 'shrimp, dressed' is a complete order.
The gravy-soaked roast-beef shreds from the pan, ordered on a po-boy (said DAY-bree).
A little something extra thrown in for free (said LAN-yap); used for any bonus.
Louis Armstrong's letter sign-off, a nod to the Monday red beans tradition that grew out of wash day.
A frozen Kool-Aid cup sold from a neighbor's front door; also called a frozen cup or cold cup.
Yakamein, the beef-noodle soup with egg and green onion sold at second lines as a hangover cure.
The pink vanilla-almond sno-ball flavor topped with condensed milk; it's a 'sno-ball', never a snow cone.
Finding the plastic baby in your king cake slice; whoever gets it buys the next cake.

designCues.cue: King cake sanding-sugar triad: purple #5B2C83, green #00843D and gold #F2B900 as glittering crystals over braided cinnamon-dough brown, not flat Carnival blocks.
designCues.source: The colored sugar on king cakes, in the Carnival colors Rex introduced in 1872.
designCues.use: Use a sugar-crystal speckle print or metallic-fleck knit for the January drop so it reads as cake rather than generic Mardi Gras.

designCues.source: The pink nectar sno-ball at Hansen's and neighborhood stands.
designCues.use: A spring and summer colorway against Pelicans navy #0C2340 for shorts and sneaker accents that only locals will decode.

designCues.cue: Boiled-crawfish red #C2401F over a newspaper-covered boil table.
designCues.source: Backyard crawfish boils poured out onto newsprint from March to May.
designCues.use: Use it for late-season and play-in warmups with a newsprint-grain texture, and never reproduce real newspaper mastheads.

designCues.cue: Powdered sugar dusted over chicory-coffee brown (base #3B2A20).
designCues.source: Beignets and café au lait, the French Market breakfast every local has eaten.
designCues.use: A soft sugar-dust gradient on dark fleece, with no Café du Monde awning stripes or logos.

designCues.cue: Waxed white butcher-paper wrap with a hand-written 'dressed' order ticket.
designCues.source: How po-boy shops wrap and ticket every sandwich, and the 1929 streetcar-strike 'poor boy' origin.
designCues.use: Use it for packaging, hangtags and shoebox tissue, with the strike origin printed inside the box.

designCues.cue: Hand-painted lettering from corner-store, po-boy and sno-ball stand signs: chunky brush capitals, drop shadows, hand-ruled menu boards.
designCues.source: Neighborhood corner stores and seasonal stands across the city.
designCues.use: Commission New Orleans sign painters to letter collection names and wordmarks, and credit them on the tag.

designCues.cue: The tiny plastic king cake baby as a hidden detail.
designCues.source: The baby baked into every king cake, and the Pelicans' own King Cake Baby mascot.
designCues.use: Hide it inside a collar, under a tongue or on a waistband tab; the mascot is team-owned IP, so it is clear to use.

designCues.cue: Red-bean mosaic: dried beans set like beadwork to form images.
designCues.source: Krewe of Red Beans costumes for the Lundi Gras Red Beans Parade.
designCues.use: Commission and pay krewe bean artists for an original graphic, and don't imitate Black Masking Indian beadwork.

productHooks: Twelfth Night Pack (Jan 6, 2027): a sanding-sugar knit warmup and tee in purple, green and gold, with a hidden King Cake Baby on the waistband, sold in a king-cake-style box next to a paid, co-branded cake from a local bakery such as Dong Phuong.
'Dressed' Pelicans hoodie and tee shipped in waxed butcher paper with an order-ticket hangtag and the 1929 'poor boy' story inside, launched at the November Oak Street Po-Boy Festival.

Nectar Cream colorway (pink #F5A3C7 on navy) for spring shorts, slides and, if his Jordan Brand signature line is still active, a Zion Williamson player-edition sneaker, launched with a paid sno-ball stand collab.
Red Beans Monday tee for Monday home games, designed with Krewe of Red Beans artists, with proceeds to Feed the Second Line.
Crawfish Season stretch-run pack: boiled-crawfish red warmups with a newsprint texture, timed to Lent and the Jazz Fest window.
Tết x Carnival capsule co-designed with Vietnamese New Orleanian artists and launched at the Mary Queen of Vietnam festival weekend.
watchouts: Food brands are third-party IP. Café du Monde, Hubig's (Savory Simon), Zapp's (Utz), Barq's (Coca-Cola), Crystal (Baumer Foods), Camellia, Leidenheimer, Zatarain's (McCormick) and Kool-Aid (Kraft Heinz) all need licenses, so no lookalike trade dress. 'Red Beans and Ricely Yours' is tied to Louis Armstrong's legacy and needs clearance.

Second-line clubs, Black Masking Indian suits and the Holy Thursday table are Black community traditions. Don't lift club names, beadwork or vendors' identities; credit and pay culture bearers directly or through Feed the Second Line.
Voodoo is a living religion: skip voodoo-doll and 'Voodoo' chip gimmicks even though they're everywhere in the tourist food trade.
Partner conflicts: Smoothie King holds the arena naming rights and Gayle Benson owns Faubourg Brewing, so clear beverage categories with the team, and never revive Dixie Beer marks.

Tremé, the Seventh Ward and Central City face displacement, and the Claiborne overpass is still an open wound. Product that borrows their food without sending money back will be called out, and there should be no Katrina or Ida puns.
